name: Robert Maxwell
role: British media proprietor (Pergamon Press, Mirror Group) and Labour MP for Buckingham (1964–1970)
summary: Maxwell sat as a Labour backbencher from 1964 to 1970, where his recorded positions were pro-technology and planning-minded on economics, strongly in favour of Britain joining the European Community, hostile to an independent British nuclear deterrent, and critical of the 1968 Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia while urging that detente be kept. Little of his stated political thinking from his later career as a publisher and newspaper owner is available in his own words, so most statements have no recorded position.

public-ownership.rationale: He voted Aye on steel nationalisation on 6 May 1965 (310-306), on the Iron and Steel Bill's second reading on 25 July 1966 (328-247) and in 1969.

unions-good.rationale: He voted Aye on the second reading of the Trade Disputes Bill on 16 February 1965 (310-286), which restored trade unions' immunity in trade disputes.

class-collaboration.rationale: In the debate on the Address on 21 April 1966 he welcomed the Government's return to 'the vital voluntary principle on which negotiations between trade unions and employers have been built up over almost a century', saying success depended on 'striking a bargain with the trade unions to accept a new and important principle for themselves, namely, that they also have a responsibility for productivity', in return for the pledge of full employment.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: On 10 May 1967 he voted Aye on the motion supporting Britain's application to join the European Communities (488-62).

reviewHistory.rationale: Contested: backed Britain joining the European Communities (10 May 1967), but also argued that supranationality had ended with Hallstein's resignation; he did not speak to pooling sovereignty itself.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: On 10 May 1967 he voted Aye on the motion supporting Britain's application to join the European Communities (488-62).
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

death-penalty.rationale: He voted Aye on the second reading of the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Bill on 21 December 1964 (355-170) and again on 16 December 1969 (343-185) to make abolition permanent.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: In the 6 April 1965 Commons debate he called the TSR2 a product of the former government's 'stupid desire' to keep a 'so-called independent nuclear deterrent' and welcomed its cancellation.

party-own-road.rationale: In the 26 August 1968 debate he called the Soviet invasion illegal and treacherous and described the Czech party's pending conference as set to clear out Stalinists and renew itself, which the Russians opposed because they wanted orders taken from the top. He sided with the Czech party deciding its own course, though he did not state the general principle.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: He voted Aye on the second reading of the Divorce Reform Bill on 9 February 1968 (159-63).

defeat-communism.rationale: In the 26 August 1968 Commons debate on the invasion of Czechoslovakia he condemned the Soviet invasion but warned against using it to revive the cold war, said it would be wrong to abandon detente, and opposed turning the Czech cause into a weapon for stiffening NATO against the Warsaw Pact. This points to coexistence and detente, not defeating communism.

notes: Searches of his Hansard contributions (1964–1970) found speeches mainly on technology, aviation, air pollution, parliamentary catering and the economy, with few statements that match the test's statements. His later statements as a newspaper owner were not found in primary form, and positions attributed to him in secondary accounts (for example on the miners' strike or on Israel) were not used. Votes: the 1964-70 debate files hold division lists as HTML tables of names; he appears in about 480 divisions. Read by theme (the death penalty, steel nationalisation, the Divorce Reform Bill, the 1967 EEC application, the Trade Disputes Bill, defence, prices and incomes): these votes replace his words for pool-sovereignty, and add death-penalty, public-ownership, no-fault-divorce and unions-good. The Sexual Offences Bill (1966) and Abortion Act (1967) divisions do not list him. His 21 April 1966 speech on voluntary pay bargaining adds class-collaboration.
